Elden Ring: Nightreign is both a continuation and a redefinition of what FromSoftware has built over the years. It retains the punishing precision and layered combat of its predecessors, while experimenting with roguelite structure and more dynamic character progression. The result is an experience that pushes the limits of the Souls formula in some bold and interesting ways.

At the core of Nightreign lies its combat system, arguably the strongest FromSoft has produced to date, created by retaining the best combat elements of Elden Ring and Sekiro. Each class feels distinct, not just in stats or equipment, but in how they approach fights, control space, and recover from mistakes. The addition of invincibility frames on most class abilities adds a satisfying layer of decision-making to defensive play, rewarding timing and precision without punishing creativity. Boss design is a consistent highlight: the Nightlords are some of the best fights across FromSoftware's entire catalog. Many of these encounters are visually stunning and mechanically complex, and the final Nightlord fight is a masterpiece - cinematic and brutal.

However, the game lacks long-term replayability in its current state. For a roguelite experience, Nightreign offers surprisingly little randomness. After enough runs, most item placements, encounter types, and even optimal routes become predictable. This deterministic feel is reinforced by the relic system - while the relics themselves are compelling, the best ones are almost always locked behind bosses or Remembrances, which hurts the variety of late-game builds. Common enemy diversity is also limited, and shielded foes are overrepresented relative to the game's fast-paced design.

The online experience is one of the game's weaker points. Matchmaking has arbitrary restrictions - notably, players with active Remembrances can't match together, which fragments the player base. The peer-to-peer infrastructure often results in inconsistent latency, which is a serious issue in a game so reliant on dodge timing. There's also no penalty for leaving a match, which creates an incentive to fish for events that can only be accessed through random chance by leaving early. Offline play is possible, but beating the Nightlords solo is a really tall task for most players, especially the ones not well-versed enough on FromSoft combat.

Despite its flaws, Nightreign is a bold and mostly brilliant addition to the Elden Ring universe. It shows FromSoft still has plenty of ideas and isn't afraid to experiment with structure, systems, and tone. If you're looking for one of the most refined and intense combat experiences in the genre mixed with some engaging co-op, it delivers without compromise. But be aware: the game will not hold your hand, it requires quite a bit of resilience, skill and teamplay to overcome its challenges.


[h1]The Good[/h1]
+ Combat is exceptional, responsive, and deeply satisfying
+ Each class is mechanically distinct and offers something unique to the table
+ Most class abilities have generous i-frames, which enhances their strategic uses
+ Solo play is both viable and enjoyable while also being quite challenging
+ Nightlords are very unique fights and rank among FromSoft's best boss designs
+ Relics that alter core character abilities are an interesting way to add some permanent power between runs
+ Archer archetype (Ironeye) is finally well-realized and fun to play


[h1]The Neutral[/h1]
* Low variety of common enemies diminishes run diversity
* Lack of enough randomness leads to many predictable runs
* Best relics being guaranteed drops from Nightlords and Remembrances reduces build variety


[h1]The Bad[/h1]
- Peer-to-peer network model is too inconsistent for such a timing-based game, they should swap to dedicated servers
- Matchmaking is in a bad spot, mainly because of arbitrary restrictions such as only a single player having a Remembrance active per lobby and because there is no penalty for leaving an ongoing game
- Shifting Earth events can only be accessed through random chance, which is fine by itself, but coupled with the fact that there are multiple achievements related to them and there is no penalty for leaving a game it can have a bad effect on the quality of matches

You are playing Elden Ring by all means, but there is a catch:

Gameplay and progress - You are in a run against time, you and your mates must progress quickly through various zones to clear enemies and level up. Your main focus is getting stronger, so in short: High level and better equipment. 
Essentially, you need to clear bosses or tough enemies, not just random foes. One of the most important locations is the Churches of Marika, you need these to max out your flask charges. If you die, you can get revived, if you dont get revived, you lose one level but you can recover your runes and level up later at a site of grace.


Gear - Just like ER , your gear consists of Main armament, Secondary Armament, Amulets and Usables. These come in different rarities and have different effects. (NOTE - ALL WEAPONS HAVE DIFFERENT ATTRIBUTES, ASHES OF WAR OR EFFECTS, WITH SOME EXCEPTIONS)
Your best bet here is to combine whatever is good for the class/character you picked, so just because a weapon is "good" by itself, doesnt mean it will help you personally if it doesnt provide the right buff.
A good thing about this, is that although you wont use a weapon, that gear can still give you passive effects that can be really useful later on, so you can still pick-up an item or weapon for certain pros even if you wont use it. 
What will also greatly impact your gameplay are the "relics". They are passive effects and buffs you get in the lobby (Roundtable) to get your stats a boost before getting into the match.

Classes - Each class is unique and requires a certain playstyle. Some classes use more specific weapons with specific buffs (which you find through the game) and certain relics can boost their stats during matches. All classes have a skill and an ultimate that provides different advantages, so yes, team composition does matter.

Revive - You can revive your mates by attacking them, and dealing massive damage can instantly bring them back (Some ultimates like the Wylder`s can instantly get back up a down mate if used right).

So far, its a really fun game if played with friends and focus on the nice aspects. Some bosses are ridiculous (I am looking at you putrid tree) and some bosses are gorgeous.
Enjoy.

Honestly, I am not a big fan of Souls games. I for one don't like the gritty you're-gonna-die aesthetic, and they're also just too difficult for my liking (ooh skill issue oooh whatever). However, my friend did buy me this one, and I have to say that I've been pleasantly surprised. Having actual functional multiplayer is a huge upgrade from all of the other FromSoft games, and archery being legitimately viable (unlike Elden Ring) is great. Nightreign is obviously a great game, but it sets itself apart from other titles in that even for non-Souls fans, it's fun.

Rarely writing the reviews, but that's a unique occasion I couldn't just ignore. I'm a huge FromSoftware games fan. Have beaten the game solo (haven't registered a single coop run) in less than 37 hours, got 32 out of 37 achievements (the ones left are probably for the remembrances, no interest in [spoiler] beating a night lord with the Revenant/Recluse, which are just not the classes I enjoy playing [/spoiler] ). And I've got to say -- it's boring. I understand the game was designed for a coop play. I understand I probably missed a lot of so called "coop fun". But in the same time, the previous studio's masterpieces were not about rush, not about narrowing circle area, and most of all not about RNG. The atmosphere of exploration and discovery is just lost. Overall the experience, while has decent positive aspects, is just frustrating. I enjoyed the strategic aspect related to time pressure to some extent, but the build creating system based on pure grinding simply repels. All in all I personally wish to see less games like this from the guys who created such masterpieces in the past.
